In a corner, hanging from a nail, he saw an old cloak made of patches. "What is this?" he asked. Ayāz answered, "This is me, in all my helplessness and lowliness. All that beauty and adornment, all that rank and delight, is you. When I look at this, I see my own weakness and know my worth. When I look at that, I see you and know it is yours, so I rejoice and lift my head."

### In short

- Allah let Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ live in Paradise and enjoy all of it, except one tree.
- Eating from that tree would make them wrongdoers who harm themselves and overstep Allah's limits.
- Ādam was made from every kind of earth, which is why human natures differ so widely.
- His honour came from Allah's nurture, not from his clay. Remembering one's lowly root keeps a person humble.

20.text:
Shayṭān now sets to work: "Then Satan tempted them in order to expose what was hidden of their nakedness. He said, “Your Lord has forbidden this tree to you only to prevent you from becoming angels or immortals.”" He envied Ādam and his wife and plotted against them, whispering and suggesting treachery. He wanted to strip them of the favours and the fine clothing they enjoyed.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then Satan tempted them"**: Satan, that is Iblīs, whispered to them to eat from the tree.

**"in order to expose what was hidden of their nakedness"**: to bring into view what had been covered from them. The Arabic for "hidden", wūriya, is on the pattern fūʿila and comes from al-muwārā, "covering". One explanation says they had been covered by a garment of light.

**"He said, “Your Lord has forbidden this tree to you only"**: he spoke lies and falsehood to Ādam and Eve.

**"to prevent you from becoming angels or immortals.”"** The meaning is, so that you do not become angels or live here forever. If you eat from this tree, he claimed, you will gain both. One explanation describes these angels as those who teach good and evil in Paradise. The word for "angels", malakayn, may also be read malikayn, "kings". He made immortality sound like the natural result of eating, as another verse shows: "But Satan whispered to him, saying, “O Adam! Shall I show you the Tree of Immortality and a kingdom that does not fade away?”" (20:120).

The construction here means "so that you do not". The same form appears in "Allah makes ˹this˺ clear to you so you do not go astray" (4:176). It appears too in "He has placed into the earth firm mountains, so it does not shake with you" (16:15).

### Shayṭān's oldest trick

Paradise in all its breadth lay open to Ādam and his wife. It held countless good things, and they were free to enjoy them as they liked. Among all those permitted things, only one was forbidden. Shayṭān made that single ban his point of attack. He told them that the thing kept from them was the most important thing in Paradise, holding the whole secret of holiness and eternity. Worn down by his constant urging, they finally ate the forbidden fruit. The result was the reverse of what they had hoped. Their disobedience stripped the cloak of safety from their bodies. They became helpless in a world where they had enjoyed every comfort and complete safety.

This shows the special weapon Shayṭān uses to draw people away from Allah's grace and help. He makes the wide world of lawful gifts look small, and blows up the importance of the few forbidden things. He dresses them up attractively and keeps assuring people of the great benefits hidden in them. He also suits his approach to each person's tastes and circumstances.

- He leads some astray by making them dislike wholesome food and telling them that wine is the way to fine health.
- A man may see that he should strengthen his own position to overcome a rival. Shayṭān whispers that the surest way to win is to launch destructive attacks on him.
- Another has every chance to improve himself. Shayṭān teaches him that protests and demands are the shortest road to success.
- Yet another has countless religious tasks he could carry out without any clash with the government of the day. Shayṭān plants the idea that Islam's complete system can prevail across the country only once un-Islamic rulers are toppled.

### Allah's care, even in the fall

Even this is a mark of Allah's care and generosity. Ādam and his wife sinned, yet He laid it at the door of Shayṭān's whispering. Then He increased His care, for their nakedness was exposed to them and not to others.

It is said that Ādam and Iblīs met afterwards. Ādam said, "You wretch! Do you know what you did to me, and what dust you stirred up on my road?" Iblīs answered, "Ādam, suppose I led you off the road. Then tell me, who led me off the road?"

### Appetite and pride

Both turned away from the command, but there is a difference between them. Ādam slipped through appetite, and Iblīs slipped through pride. Pride is worse than giving in to an appetite. When a sin comes from appetite there is room for pardon. When a sin comes from pride, faith is lost in it. A report says, "Magnificence is My cloak and tremendousness My shawl. Whoever contends with Me over either, I will smash him."

### In short

- Out of envy, Shayṭān whispered to Ādam and his wife, to strip them of the covering and comforts they enjoyed.
- He lied that the tree would make them angels or immortals.
- His oldest trick is to make the lawful look small and the few forbidden things look grand, shaped to each person's tastes.
- Ādam slipped through appetite, which leaves room for pardon. Iblīs slipped through pride, which destroys faith.

21.text:
Shayṭān backed his lie with an oath: "And he swore to them, “I am truly your sincere advisor.”" He swore to Ādam and his wife by Allah that he wanted nothing but their good.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And he swore to them"**: the word is qāsamahumā, "he swore to the two of them", and he swore by Allah.

**"“I am truly your sincere advisor.”"** In one paraphrase his words are: "By Allah, I am a sincere adviser to you both, Ādam and Eve, in what I direct you to." His sincerity was claimed "in this matter", and what he swore to was that this was the tree of immortality. He added, in effect, "I was here before you, so I know this place better." Qatādah said that Shayṭān swore by Allah, saying, "I was created before you, and I know more than you do. So follow me, and I will guide you."

### Can a believer be deceived?

It is a fact that a believer in Allah may sometimes fall victim to deceit. Ādam and his wife believed in Allah, and Shayṭān swore by Allah to win them over.

### In short

- Shayṭān swore by Allah that he was a sincere adviser to Ādam and his wife.
- He claimed the authority of seniority: he was created first and knew the place better.
- A believer in Allah can sometimes be taken in by deceit.

22.text:
The deception worked: "So he brought about their fall through deception. And when they tasted of the tree, their nakedness was exposed to them, prompting them to cover themselves with leaves from Paradise. Then their Lord called out to them, “Did I not forbid you from that tree and ˹did I not˺ tell you that Satan is your sworn enemy?”" Shayṭān lured them with falsehood and lies until they ate. At once they lost their covering and heard their Lord's reproach.

### Phrase by phrase

**"So he brought about their fall through deception."** He led them on by guile. He lowered their rank through his delusion, bringing them down from their high position by trickery, until they ate from the tree.

**"And when they tasted of the tree"** means when they ate of it.

**"their nakedness was exposed to them"**: the front and back private parts of each became visible to the other. Each is called sawʾah, "shameful", because its exposure shames (yasūʾu) the person. Wahb ibn Munabbih commented on the later phrase "stripping them of their clothing" (7:27). He said a light once covered the private parts of Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ (Eve), so neither could see the other's. Eating from the tree removed it, and their private parts became visible to them. Ibn Jarīr reported this with an authentic chain.

**"prompting them to cover themselves with leaves from Paradise"**: out of shame they began to stick leaves onto themselves to cover up. Ibn ʿAbbās said these were fig leaves, and this has an authentic chain to him. Mujāhid said they made the leaves into a garment.

**"Then their Lord called out to them"**: "O Ādam and Eve".

**"“Did I not forbid you from that tree and ˹did I not˺ tell you that Satan is your sworn enemy?”"** The question is really a statement: I did forbid you to eat from that tree, and I did warn you. Satan, that is Iblīs, is an enemy whose hostility is plain.

### Why did Ādam run?

According to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Ādam was as tall as a palm tree and had a thick head of hair. When he committed his error his private part appeared to him, though he had never seen it before. He ran through Paradise in fright until a tree caught him by the head. He said to it, "Let me go," but it answered, "No, I will not let you go." Then his Lord called him: "Ādam, are you running away from Me?" He said, "My Lord, I felt ashamed before You."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Marduwyah collected this through several chains, from al-Ḥasan from Ubayy, who traced it back to the Prophet ﷺ. Even so, it is more correct to treat it as Ubayy's own statement.

### The inner reading: one taste, and a kingdom lost

Whoever follows the soul's appetite against the command of the Real is held back from the Real, and does not reach the appetite either. Ādam the Chosen had taken no more than a taste of the forbidden tree when the whip of rebuke fell on his head and his state changed. He neither fully satisfied the appetite nor kept Allah's approval. When he looked again there was no crown on his head and no robe on his body. Before, he had seen himself seated on the throne of chosenness, leaning on the cushion of vicegerency, dressed in the robes and ornaments of Paradise. Now he saw himself cut off from all of it, naked and hungry, in need of a single leaf.

Blessed are the noble ones who set out early like kings and took their rest like the poor! As the verse says, "Wonder not at my abasement. I am he with whose lifeblood time sported, then abased."

Then the command came: "Ādam, you could not enjoy all those blessings without hardship and toil. Now go to the house of trial and adversity. Work, sow seeds, take pains and be patient." Ādam said, "All of this is a small thing, if one day I am let back to this Threshold." He grieved over the pain in his heart and laid his need and weakness on the palms of remorse. Then he wept and made the plea of the next verse.

### In short

- Shayṭān brought Ādam and his wife down from their high rank by lies and trickery.
- When they ate, the light that covered them was gone. They saw their nakedness and covered themselves with leaves, fig leaves in one report.
- Allah reminded them that He had forbidden the tree and warned them of Shayṭān's open enmity.
- Following an appetite against Allah's command loses both the appetite and Allah's approval.

23.text:
Unlike Iblīs, Ādam and his wife turned straight back to their Lord: "They replied, “Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers.”" They admitted their fault without excuses and asked for forgiveness and mercy.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They replied, “Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves."** We have harmed ourselves by our disobedience, by doing what You forbade us. Ādam and Eve both said it.

**"If You do not forgive us"** means if You do not overlook our wrongdoing.

**"and have mercy on us"**: by sparing us punishment.

**"we will certainly be losers.”"** We will be among the lost, those tricked into earning punishment, who lose their share of both this world and the Hereafter. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim also commented on this plea.

### Two requests, two answers

ʿAbd ar-Razzāq reported from Qatādah that Ādam said, "My Lord, what if I repent and seek forgiveness?" Allah said, "Then I will admit you into Paradise." Shayṭān, for his part, asked not for forgiveness but for respite. Each of them was given what he asked for.

### The inner reading: the plea of the dust

Ādam's plea is drawn out in the language of intimate prayer.

"O Allah, if we weep, weeping for You is sweet. If we lament before You, our lament is fitting. O Allah, what comes from dust but error? What is born of a flaw but disloyalty? And what comes from the Generous but faithfulness? O Allah, we have come back with both hands empty. What would it cost You to lay balm on the wounded?"

"O Allah, You are the treasure of the poor and the provision of the distressed. You are the refuge of those who flee and the One who takes the hand of the helpless. You created us and saw the flawed jewel, yet You chose it and bought it with all its faults. You raised us up when no one asked You to. Now that You have raised us, do not cast us down. Keep us in the shade of Your gentleness, and leave us to nothing but Your bounty."

"If You water, it was You who planted. If You level the foundation, it was You who raised it. I, the servant, am only what You made of me. Do not throw me down, for You lifted me up."

### In short

- Ādam and his wife admitted their wrong at once, without excuses, and asked for forgiveness and mercy.
- They knew that without Allah's forgiveness they would lose both this world and the Hereafter.
- Ādam asked for forgiveness and Shayṭān asked for respite, and each was given what he asked.

24.text:
The sentence of descent follows: "Allah said, “Descend as enemies to each other. You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay.”" Everyone in this story was sent down from Paradise to the earth. There the enmity begun in Paradise would play out, and there each person would have a home and provision until a fixed term.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah said, “Descend"** means go down from Paradise to the earth. One report says the command was given to four: Ādam, Ḥawwāʾ (Eve), Iblīs and the snake. Other scholars leave the snake out. Allah knows best. One explanation names Ādam, Eve, the serpent and the peacock. Another says it means Ādam and Eve, together with all the descendants they carried within them. Another verse says, "Descend, both of you, from here together ˹with Satan˺ as enemies to each other" (20:123).

**"as enemies to each other."** The enmity is chiefly between Ādam and Iblīs, and Ḥawwāʾ follows Ādam in it. If the story of the snake is true, the snake is one of Iblīs's followers. Another explanation is that Ādam's descendants will be enemies to one another, because of the wrongs they do each other.

**"You will find in the earth a residence"**: a dwelling, a shelter and a place to settle.

**"and provision for your appointed stay.”"** You will enjoy what is in the earth for a while, until death, when your terms of life are complete. These terms are known and fixed. They were recorded by the Pen, counted out by Allah's decree and written in the First Record.

### Where did they land?

Some scholars named the places on earth where they came down. These accounts come from the Israelite tales, and only Allah knows whether they are true. If knowing these places were of any use to people in their religion or their worldly life, Allah would have mentioned them in His Book. His Messenger ﷺ would have mentioned them too.

### An enmity that lasts until the Last Day

Ādam and Shayṭān were both sent to earth as enemies, and the battle between them will go on until Doomsday. Shayṭān strives without rest to bring people onto his path and to rob them of Allah's grace, as he himself was robbed of it. A person should stand against him and wreck his plans. He should ignore Shayṭān's call and hurry to answer the call of Allah.

This struggle shows itself in humanity splitting into two groups. Some give in to Shayṭān's lures and fall in line behind him. Those who answer Allah's call run the risk that all of Shayṭān's companions will plot to slander and defeat them. In every age the true devotees of truth, always few in number, have suffered the bitterest hostility from those who deny the truth. The reason is Shayṭān's enmity. He turns people against the true believers and fills their hearts with a burning hatred for them. Some people become his tools and set about harassing those devoted to the truth.

Shayṭān's real sin was his refusal to acknowledge the favour Allah had given Ādam. He tries to create the same temperament in every human being.

- He stirs up the young to deny their elders the regard they are due.
- In social or business dealings, when one party is bound by honour to give the other his due, Shayṭān persuades him to break his word.
- When a servant of Allah brings the message of truth, Shayṭān plants all kinds of doubts in people's hearts so that they refuse it.
- In a dispute where one side is ready to pay what fits its means, Shayṭān quietly urges the other side to refuse. He prompts demands so huge that they cannot be met, so the quarrel goes on.

In this way, through Shayṭān's misguidance, enmity spreads everywhere. Two opposing camps form among human beings, and Shayṭān makes sure their confrontation never ends.

### In short

- Ādam, Ḥawwāʾ and Iblīs, with the snake in some reports, were sent down to earth, with enmity between humankind and Shayṭān.
- The earth gives each person a home and provision until a term that Allah has fixed and recorded.
- Accounts of where they landed come from Israelite tales. Such knowledge has no use, or Allah and His Messenger ﷺ would have given it.
- The struggle with Shayṭān runs until the Last Day and splits people into two camps.

25.text:
The verse completes the sentence on the earth: "He added, “There you will live, there you will die, and from there you will be resurrected.”" Allah addressed Ādam, Eve and their descendants. He made the earth the home of the children of Ādam for the rest of this worldly life, and the place of their return.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He added, “There you will live"**: on the earth, for the length of time Allah decrees for you.

**"there you will die"**: on the earth too, and there you will be buried in your graves.

**"and from there you will be resurrected.”"** From the earth you will be brought out of your graves on the Day of Judgement and returned to life. The verb can be read actively, takhrujūn, "you will come forth", or passively, tukhrajūn, "you will be brought forth". The verse is like another: "From the earth We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you back again" (20:55).

### What comes after the resurrection?

On the Day of Resurrection Allah will gather the first and the last of all creatures. He will then reward or punish each person according to what he or she did.

### In short

- The earth is humanity's home in life, its grave in death, and the place from which it will be raised.
- At the resurrection Allah will gather all creation and repay each person for his or her deeds.

26.text:
The story of Ādam and Shayṭān has just been told. The first result of Shayṭān's prompting was that the heavenly clothing of Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ (Eve) fell away, leaving them to hide themselves with leaves. Now Allah addresses all their descendants: "O children of Adam! We have provided for you clothing to cover your nakedness and as an adornment. However, the best clothing is righteousness. This is one of Allah’s bounties, so perhaps you will be mindful". The clothes people wear are a great blessing, and they should know its worth. Three kinds of clothing are named, and the last is the best.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O children of Adam!"** The address is not to Muslims alone but to every child of Ādam. This is a sharp pointer to a fact: covering the body and wearing clothes is both a human need and a natural desire. Everyone keeps to it, whatever their religion or community.

**"We have provided for you clothing"**: the Arabic word is anzalnā, "We have sent down". Here it means "We have bestowed, We have blessed you with", or "We have created it and given it to you". The clothing need not come down from the sky ready to wear. Another verse uses the same word for iron: "And We sent down iron with its great might" (57:25), though iron is dug out of the earth, as anyone can see.

In both places, "sent down" points to something. No human planning plays any part in what descends from the heavens. In the same way, the basic stuff of clothing, such as cotton, wool and fur, owes nothing to human cleverness. It is a pure gift of Allah's creative power. Human skill does come in when these materials are made into garments that suit a person's taste and temperament and keep out heat and cold. Yet even the way to that skill is shown by Allah. So eyes that see reality see all of it as a gift sent down from the heavens.

**"to cover your nakedness"**: the verb yuwārī comes from muwārāt, which means to cover, hide or conceal. The word sawʾāt is the plural of sawʾah. It is used for the parts of the body that every human being, by nature, feels it bad and shameful to uncover. Allah has sent down clothing with which people can cover those parts. This first kind of clothing is essential.

**"and as an adornment"**: the word is rīsh, literally "feathers". It means everything one adorns oneself with, the outer garments worn for beauty, and this second kind is a complement to the first. Ibn Jarīr said rīsh includes furnishings and outer clothes. Another explanation takes it as property and goods, the furniture of a house. The meaning is that a simple set of clothes would be enough to cover what must be covered. But Allah has given far more than that. He has blessed people with clothes that make them look handsome, decent, neat and civilised.

**"However, the best clothing is righteousness."** This is libās at-taqwā, "the clothing of taqwā", meaning mindfulness and fear of Allah. In some readings (qirāʾāt) the word libās ends in -a, joining it to the earlier "clothing". Read with "We have sent down", it then means: We have sent down a third clothing, the clothing of taqwā. In the well-known reading it ends in -u and begins a new sentence: everyone knows the two kinds of clothing just named, but there is a third, the clothing of taqwā, and that is the best of all.

Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿUrwah ibn az-Zubayr explained the clothing of taqwā as right conduct, good deeds and fear of Allah. Others describe it as righteous deeds and virtuous traits. Others say it is the clothing of declaring Allah's Oneness and of self-restraint, which is better than clothes of cotton. Others again say it means following what Allah commands and keeping away from what He has not allowed, which is better than any physical clothing. ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said, "When someone fears Allah, Allah covers his faults. Hence 'the clothing of taqwā'."

**"This is one of Allah’s bounties"**: the clothing mentioned here is among the signs of Allah. It is one of His marvels and a proof of His power over everything.

**"so perhaps you will be mindful"**: so that people may take heed, remember Allah's blessings to them, give thanks for them and believe. In the Arabic, the address here shifts from "you" to "they".

### What is clothing for?

Two uses of clothing are named here. The first is to cover the parts of the body that must be covered (satr). The second is to protect against heat and cold and to adorn the body. Covering is mentioned first. This shows that the real purpose of human clothing is to cover the ʿawrah, the private parts (satr al-ʿawrah).

Covering is also what marks humans off from animals. An animal's clothing is made by nature a part of its body, and it serves to protect it from heat and cold or to make it beautiful. No elaborate arrangement covers its private parts. Even so, the parts of an animal's body are placed so that they do not stay fully exposed. Some have the screen of a tail, and many others have other things that block the view.

This mention of clothing comes straight after the story of how Shayṭān led Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ astray. That placing shows that for human beings to be naked, or to expose their shame before others, is a sign of utter disgrace and the worst indecency. It also opens the way to every kind of evil and disorder.

### The tempter of Ādam and Eve still stalks

Shayṭān's first attack on humankind came through this opening, when their clothing fell from where it belonged. Even today, when Shayṭān wants to confuse and waylay people through his accomplices, he puts on a stylish front. He dresses it up as trendy, hip, hot or cool. In the end he pulls people out of their homes and into the streets and alleys, naked or nearly so. It seems that what Shayṭān calls modern progress cannot happen until women are robbed of their sense of shame and modesty and made to parade about almost nude.

### Why is covering the first duty after faith?

Shayṭān sensed this weakness in human beings and aimed his first assault at their covering. The Sharīʿah of Islam is charged with planting, protecting and bringing to flower every good in its people. So it took the matter very seriously and made covering the body the first duty after īmān, faith. Ṣalāh, ṣawm (fasting) and duties like them come after it.

Al-Fārūq al-Aʿẓam reported that the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever puts on a new garment should say a supplication as he does so. In it he praises Allah, who gave him clothes to cover what must be covered and to look well in throughout his life.

The Prophet ﷺ also said that whoever puts on a new garment and gives the old one in ṣadaqah, charity, to someone poor and needy, comes under Allah's protection and care in every state of his life and death. This is recorded in the Musnad of Aḥmad. This hadith too recalls the two purposes for which Allah created human clothing.

### Was the first man naked?

The story of Ādam and the words of the Qur'an make one thing clear. Covering the body and wearing clothes is a natural desire and an inborn need of human beings, and it has been with them since the very beginning. Some claim that the first man went about naked and invented clothing only after passing through stages of evolution. That claim is plainly false.

### What is the clothing of taqwā?

Physical clothing covers what must be covered, protects from heat and cold, and gives beauty. In just the same way there is a spiritual clothing: right and fitting conduct, good deeds and fear of Allah. This clothing of taqwā hides human weaknesses and moral failings. It saves a person from hardship now and from loss at the end. That is why it is the best clothing anyone can wear.

Allah has made the world so that its outward things are signs of an inner reality. By thinking about what is outward, a person can reach hidden truths. Clothing is one such sign. Allah gave people clothes that protect them and also improve their looks and standing. This shows that the human spirit needs a clothing too. That clothing is taqwā, righteousness born of the fear of Allah, and it is a person's inner self. It shields him from Shayṭān's attacks. It also refines his inner self and makes him fit to live in the fine and beautiful world of Paradise.

What, then, is taqwā? It includes:

- Fearing Allah and acknowledging the truth.
- Applying the same standard to oneself as to others.
- Seeing oneself as Allah's subject.
- Behaving with modesty and humility.
- Living for the Hereafter rather than wandering lost in the world.

When a person grows these virtues, he clothes his inner self. The outer body is covered with a garment of cloth, and the soul is clothed in taqwā. If he behaves in the opposite way, it is as if he were stripping his inner self bare.

### Can a hidden deed stay hidden?

The verse also hints that an evildoer who has no fear of Allah and no care for right conduct will be disgraced in the end, however well he covers himself. Ibn Jarīr reported from ʿUthmān al-Ghanī that the Prophet ﷺ swore by Allah, in whose hand is Muhammad's life. Whatever a person does in secret, he said, Allah wraps around him like a sheet and makes known. If the deed is good its good shows, and if it is evil its evil shows. Being wrapped in it like a sheet means that everyone can see it. However secretly something is done, Allah makes its effects show on the face and the body. To support his words, the Prophet ﷺ then recited this verse, from its mention of adornment and the clothing of taqwā to "This is one of Allah’s bounties".

### How should taqwā show in dress?

The phrase "clothing of taqwā" shows that even physical clothing, which covers and beautifies the body, is really meant as a way to taqwā. That aim should show in the way a person dresses.

- The parts of the body that must be covered should be fully covered, so that one's modesty stays hidden.
- Clothes should not be so tight that the body looks naked through them.
- Dress should carry no air of pride and arrogance. It should reflect modesty and humility.
- It should not be extravagant. The cloth used should be cut to need.
- Women's dress should not be masculine and men's dress should not be feminine, for this is hateful in Allah's sight.
- One should not copy others' dress in a way that signals a departure from the settled ways of one's own community.

Along with all this comes the vital need to set one's morals and deeds right, and that is the real aim of clothing. That is why the verse ends with an invitation to understand, so that people may take the advice to heart.

### In short

- Clothing is a blessing to every child of Ādam. Covering the body is a human need and a natural desire, not a late invention.
- Allah "sent down" clothing: its raw materials are His gift, and even the skill to make garments comes from His guidance.
- Clothing covers and adorns. Covering comes first, and after faith it is the first duty.
- The best clothing is taqwā: right conduct, good deeds and fear of Allah, which hides faults and guards against Shayṭān.
- Dress should be modest, not tight, proud or extravagant, and should not cross between the sexes or imitate others.

27.text:
The address turns again to every child of Ādam, this time as a warning: "O children of Adam! Do not let Satan deceive you as he tempted your parents out of Paradise and caused their cover to be removed in order to expose their nakedness. Surely he and his soldiers watch you from where you cannot see them. We have made the devils allies of those who disbelieve". People should guard against Shayṭān's deception in everything they do and in every situation. Otherwise he may put them through the same trial he brought on their parents, Ādam and Eve.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O children of Adam! Do not let Satan deceive you"**: do not let Iblīs make you slip in obeying Me or lead you astray. Do not follow him, lest you fall into his temptation. He deceives by making disobedience look beautiful. He tempts people to stop covering their nakedness with clothing, or to abandon the clothing of mindfulness, taqwā.

**"as he tempted your parents out of Paradise"**: he made eating from the tree look good to Ādam and Eve, and the result was their expulsion from Paradise. Iblīs plotted to move Ādam from the home of comfort to the home of hardship and toil, which is this life.

**"and caused their cover to be removed"**: the verb yanziʿu, "stripping", describes the state they were in as they left. He took away their robe, which one explanation calls the robe of light. He caused Ādam's private parts to be uncovered after they had been hidden from him.

**"in order to expose their nakedness."** His aim was to show them their shameful parts. This points to a deep hatred, for Ādam and for all humankind.

**"Surely he and his soldiers watch you"**: the word for his soldiers is qabīl, which means a company or group. A family group bound together is called a qabīlah, a tribe, and looser groups are called qabīl. So the meaning is "he and his tribe", his army.

**"from where you cannot see them."** One explanation gives the reason as "because your breasts are their dwellings". Another explains it by their airy bodies, or by their having no colour. Either way, Shayṭān is an enemy who sees you with his helpers while you do not see them. That makes the chance of falling for their deception quite strong, so always be on your guard against him and his tribe.

**"We have made the devils allies of those who disbelieve"**: the devils are made friends, helpers and companions of those who do not believe in Allah, in Muhammad ﷺ and in the Qur'an. Against those who have faith and do good, the devils have no way in.

### An enemy from the very beginning

The warning against Iblīs and his followers rests on history. Allah reminds Ādam's children how old his hatred is, going back to their first father. That enmity was never something they could afford to forget. A similar verse says:

> "Would you then take him and his descendants as patrons instead of Me, although they are your enemy? What an evil alternative for the wrongdoers ˹to choose˺" (18:50).

### How can anyone guard against an unseen enemy?

Other verses make clear that Shayṭān's cunning web is very weak against people who keep turning to Allah and stay on guard against his tricks. The end of this verse points the same way. If the devils are made the friends and guardians of those who disbelieve, then those who believe should find it no hardship at all to keep clear of their snares.

Some righteous elders said that the defence against an enemy who sees us, while we cannot see him, is simple. Come under Allah's protection. He sees these devils and watches how they move and act, but they cannot see Him. The clothing of taqwā, described under the previous verse, also shields a person from Shayṭān's attacks.

### Can people ever see the jinn?

The statement that human beings cannot see Shayṭān describes the normal course of things. If someone saw them by way of an exception to the usual pattern, that would not contradict the verse. Authentic hadith narrations, for example, tell of jinn who came to the Prophet ﷺ, asked him questions and accepted Islam.

### In short

- Allah warns all of Ādam's children to guard against Shayṭān at all times, lest he do to them what he did to their parents.
- His ancient enmity showed when he had Ādam and Eve expelled from Paradise and stripped of their covering.
- He and his forces see people while people cannot see them, so the danger is real.
- Yet his web is weak against those who turn to Allah, and he is the ally only of those who disbelieve.
- Normally humans do not see the jinn, though authentic hadiths tell of jinn who came to the Prophet ﷺ and accepted Islam.

28.text:
This verse was revealed to root out a shameful custom of the pagan Arabs: "Whenever they commit a shameful deed, they say, “We found our forefathers doing it and Allah has commanded us to do it.” Say, “No! Allah never commands what is shameful. How can you attribute to Allah what you do not know?”" When told to stop, the idolaters defended their deeds with two arguments: their forefathers had always done it, and Allah had commanded it. The verse answers the second, and the first hardly needs an answer.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Whenever they commit a shameful deed"**: the word is fāḥishah. Most explanations say it refers here to circling the Kaʿbah naked. More broadly, fuḥsh, faḥshāʾ and fāḥishah mean any evil act whose wickedness reaches the furthest limit and is loud and clear to common sense and sound taste. That the good and bad of such acts can be known by reason is established everywhere. Other examples given are idolatry, and forbidding the dedicated animals called al-Baḥīrah, as-Sāʾibah, al-Waṣīlah and al-Ḥām.

**"they say, “We found our forefathers doing it"**: we found them practising it, so we followed their example. To give up the practice now, they felt, would be a disgrace.

**"and Allah has commanded us to do it.”"** This was a flagrant lie. They claimed that what their forefathers did was really obedience to Allah's order and law.

**"Say, “No! Allah never commands what is shameful."** Say to them, O Muhammad: the practice you indulge in is a vile sin, and Allah does not command such a thing. On the contrary, He forbids it. Commanding anything like it would go against His wisdom and against His being the Purest of the pure.

**"How can you attribute to Allah what you do not know?”"** The question is a rebuke. Do you put words into Allah's mouth that you cannot be sure He said? Or are you simply inventing things about Him?

### What was the naked ṭawāf?

Mujāhid said the idolaters used to circle the House naked, saying, "We make ṭawāf as our mothers bore us." A woman would cover her private part with something and say, "Today some or all of it may show, but whatever shows, I do not permit it." Then Allah sent down this verse.

Apart from the Quraysh, the Arabs used to make ṭawāf naked. They said they would not circle the House in clothes in which they had disobeyed Allah, so they banned wearing clothes for it. The Quraysh, known as al-Ḥums, circled in their ordinary clothes. Being servants of the sacred Ḥaram, they were exempt from this law of nakedness. An Arab who borrowed a garment from one of the Ḥums wore it for his ṭawāf. Someone who came in a new garment threw it off after the ṭawāf, and no one would wear it after him. Those with no new garment, and no loan from the Ḥums, went round naked. The Quraysh could not clothe the whole of Arabia, so most people made ṭawāf naked, men and women alike. The women usually went round in the dark of night.

The idolaters invented this practice themselves, simply following their forefathers. So lacking in sense were they that it never struck them how much worse nakedness was. It offended the House far more than their clothes could, and it offended human dignity itself.

### Is "our forefathers did it" an argument?

Their first argument was that ancestral customs must be kept, as if keeping them were good in itself. The answer is plain: blindly following ancestral custom is not reasonable. Anyone of ordinary sense can see that a practice is not justified just because one's forefathers did it. If it were, the forefathers of different peoples acted in different and even opposite ways, and every wrong practice in the world would become right and lawful. The argument did not deserve attention, and so the Qur'an did not answer it here. Some hadith narrations do answer it: a foolish act committed by one's forefathers is not worth following by any stretch of the imagination.

### Why is speaking about Allah without knowledge so serious?

Their second argument, that Allah had ordered it, was a bare lie. They were ascribing to Allah something He had never commanded, without any evidence. To attribute something to anyone without proper inquiry and authority is gross effrontery and plain injustice. Done about Allah, it is a crime and an injustice whose size cannot be imagined.

This verse does not cover the work of the qualified imams of ijtihād, independent legal reasoning. When they draw out and set down rulings from the verses of the Qur'an, they work within the warrant of the Qur'an's own words and meanings.

### How does Shayṭān make the shameful look right?

Shayṭān leads people astray by misinforming them. He made the forbidden tree look like the spring from which every advantage flowed. He comes by such harmless-looking ways that a person has no idea he is being misled. He knows all the weak points and tender places in human moral armour, and he aims at exactly those spots.

Whom does he succeed in misleading? He succeeds with:

- Those who cannot show their faith in times of trial.
- Those who do not think carefully about Allah's signs.
- Those who reject sound arguments.
- Those who will not put the demands of truth before their own inclinations.

Such people do not recognise the truth as truth if it does not serve their interests.

### In short

- The idolaters defended shameful acts, above all circling the Kaʿbah naked, by appeal to their forefathers and to a command from Allah.
- Following forefathers blindly proves nothing, since ancestors of different peoples did opposite things.
- Allah never commands what is shameful. Ascribing to Him what one does not know is an injustice beyond measure.
- Rulings that qualified scholars derive from the Qur'an's words are not speaking about Allah without knowledge.

29.text:
Against their claim, the Prophet ﷺ is told to state what Allah really commands: "Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “My Lord has commanded uprightness and dedication ˹to Him alone˺ in worship, calling upon Him with sincere devotion. Just as He first brought you into being, you will be brought to life again.”" Those who said Allah had ordered their naked ṭawāf are told that He always commands justice, not indecency or sin.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “My Lord has commanded uprightness"**: the word is al-qisṭ, which means justice, balance and moderation. Here it means conduct free of excess and of shortfall. It neither falls short of the set limits nor goes beyond them, as with every injunction of the Sharīʿah. So qisṭ takes in every act of worship and obedience, and all the general injunctions of the Sharīʿah. Others explain it as fairness, or as declaring Allah's Oneness, that there is no god but Allah.

**"and dedication ˹to Him alone˺ in worship"**: literally, "set your faces aright at every masjid". Grammatically, wa-aqīmū ("and set") is joined to the sense of "justice", as if He had said, "Be just, and set your faces." It may also be read with an implied "so turn". Most explanations take masjid here to mean prostration (sajdah, sujūd), that is, worship. One should be upright at every ṣalāh and every act of worship, prostrating purely for Allah. It could also mean taking care to face the qiblah correctly. Or it could mean making everything one says and does follow what Allah has commanded, with a direction that never wavers or drifts. On that reading the command is not limited to ṣalāh. It covers all worship, dealings and transactions. Allah commands loyalty to Him in worship in general, and in places of worship in particular.

To be straight in worship means following the messengers, who were supported by miracles, and obeying what they brought from Allah and the law they conveyed. Allah does not accept a good deed until it meets two conditions. It must be correct, in line with His law, and it must be free of shirk.

**"calling upon Him with sincere devotion."** Worship Him and call on Him alone, making your religion purely His, free of any idolatry. Nothing and no one should be joined with Him in that worship in any capacity. It should even be free of al-shirk al-khafiyy, the hidden shirk of hypocrisy and showing off (riyāʾ).

**"Just as He first brought you into being, you will be brought to life again.”"** Several explanations are given.

- Mujāhid said it means life restored after death.
- Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said that the One who started you off in this world will revive you on the Day of Resurrection.
- Qatādah said that Allah first created them out of nothing, then they died, and He will return them.
- ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said that He who made you at the start will restore you at the finish.
- Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as: He began the children of Ādam as believers and disbelievers, and He will bring them back the same way. Another explanation says He brought them into being on the Day of the Covenant as happy and wretched, knowing and denying, believing and disbelieving, and they will return in that state. This view is taken up under the next verse.

Abū Jaʿfar Ibn Jarīr preferred the explanation of ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Zayd. He supported it with a report from Ibn ʿAbbās. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood and addressed the people. He told them they would be gathered to Allah barefoot, naked and uncircumcised. Then he recited, "Just as We produced the first creation, ˹so˺ shall We reproduce it. That is a promise binding on Us" (21:104). This hadith is in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs.

The One who could create you the first time, from nothing, can surely bring you back. For His perfect power this is no effort at all. Perhaps that is why the Arabic says taʿūdūn, "you will return", and not "We shall raise you". Raising people again needs very little action.

### Outward and inward together

After the command of justice and balance, two injunctions that bear directly on the idolaters' conduct are named. "Set your faces" concerns what a person does with the body, outwardly. "Call upon Him with sincere devotion" concerns the heart. Naming both together suggests that both sides of a person must be put right and brought into line with the Sharīʿah, the outward and the inward, the physical and the spiritual.

Outward obedience (iṭāʿah) is not enough without sincerity (ikhlāṣ). Nor is sincerity of heart enough without visibly following the Sharīʿah. Everyone must bring his outward conduct into line with the Sharīʿah and also keep his inner life reserved for Allah alone. This exposes the error of those who treat Sharīʿah, outward observance, and Ṭarīqah, the inward path, as two separate roads to religion. Some even suppose it is enough to put the inner self right through the Ṭarīqah while acting against the Sharīʿah. That is a gaping error.

### Why mention the Resurrection here?

Mentioning the Resurrection at this point has a further benefit. It helps people keep the injunctions of the Sharīʿah. Knowing that there is a life to come, a Last Day, and reward or punishment for deeds is what makes the hard easy and the painful bearable. Experience shows that man is a tough customer. Without that gripping awareness, no advice will make him do right, and no legal restriction will stop him from crime.

### What does justice demand?

Justice, qisṭ, is behaviour that meets every moral standard, being exactly what it should be. Worship is a natural urge in every person. He wants to accept some Being as supreme and to bow down before Him. Justice is done here only if he worships the one true God, his Creator, Lord and Sustainer. A person also wants some Being at the centre of his convictions, and justice means making the All-Powerful Allah the ground of his trust. In the same way, accepting life after death is justice in the fullest sense. Everyone came into being out of non-being when he was born. Believing in resurrection is believing in the very reality every person has already lived through at birth.

### The inner reading: one verse holding the whole religion

This verse, from the Lord of heaven and earth, brings three things together: the realities of recognition, the signposts of practice, and the foundations of service. Through it He shows the faithful which traits of character please Him. He teaches them to worship Him beautifully and to live beautifully with His creatures, and He honours them by showing them what earns His approval. This verse is among the "all-comprehensive words" of which al-Muṣṭafā said, "I was sent with the all-comprehensive words, and knowledge was made very concise for me."

The Qur'an has many such verses. Take one: "Surely Allah is with those who shun evil and who do good ˹deeds˺" (16:128). See how much meaning so short a verse holds. "Surely Allah is with" holds all of Allah's tenderness, generosity and bounty toward His servant. "Those who shun evil" covers every kind of worship and practice the servant offers Allah. "Who do good" covers all that people owe one another in their dealings.

In the same way, all the pillars of religion, the positions of the Sharīʿah and the gates of the Ḥaqīqah are contained in this verse. It is as if the Prophet ﷺ were saying, "Allah has commanded me to be just in my dealings with the Real, with His creatures and with my own soul."

- With the Real, by acting on what He commands and forbids, and being content with whatever He decrees.
- With people, by good character and fair dealing in every transaction, while never insisting on fairness for oneself.
- With one's own soul, by resisting it, forcing it to strive and train, and closing the door on appetite and comfort.

The counterpart of this verse in the Qur'an is "Indeed, Allah commands justice, grace" (16:90).

### In short

- Allah commands qisṭ: justice and balance in worship, in dealings and in all of life, never indecency.
- Worship must be outwardly correct according to His law and inwardly sincere, free even of hidden shirk and showing off.
- Sharīʿah and Ṭarīqah are not two roads. Inner purity never excuses outward disobedience.
- The One who created people from nothing will bring them back, and remembering this makes obedience easier.

30.text:
Humanity divides into two groups: "He has guided some, while others are destined to stray. They have taken devils as their masters instead of Allah—thinking they are ˹rightly˺ guided". Allah's guidance was open to all. Some accepted it, while others turned away, followed the devils, and then came to think that their sickness was health and their error was guidance.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He has guided some"**: a group of you He has guided. He made the way to guidance easy for them and removed the barriers in their path. He honoured them with knowledge and happiness, and they are the people of the right.

**"while others are destined to stray."** Another group has earned going astray, and error is decreed for them. They have shown proof of their own wrongdoing. Allah humbled them with denial and wretchedness, and they are the people of the left.

**"They have taken devils as their masters instead of Allah"**: they made the devils their friends, helpers, patrons and even gods, bypassing Allah. In their ignorance they bound themselves to them, and so they strayed from the path of truth.

**"thinking they are ˹rightly˺ guided"**: the misguided believe they are following Allah's religion and walking a straight path.

### Were people created believers or disbelievers?

The explanation of the previous verse from Ibn ʿAbbās leads into this one. Allah began the creation of the children of Ādam with some believing and some disbelieving, as He says: "He is the One Who created you, yet some of you are disbelievers while some are believers" (64:2). He will bring them back on the Day of Resurrection as He began them.

A hadith from Ibn Masʿūd, which al-Bukhārī recorded, supports this meaning. The Prophet ﷺ swore by the One besides whom there is no god. One of you, he said, may do the deeds of the people of Paradise until only an arm's length lies between him and it. Then what was written in the Book overtakes him, and he does the deeds of the people of the Fire and enters it. Another may do the deeds of the people of the Fire until only an arm's length separates him from it. Then what was written overtakes him, and he does the deeds of the people of Paradise and enters Paradise.

If this is the correct meaning of the verse, it must be read together with other texts.

- Allah speaks of "the natural Way of Allah which He has instilled in ˹all˺ people" (30:30).
- Abū Hurayrah reported in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs that the Prophet ﷺ said every child is born upon the fiṭrah, the natural state, and it is his parents who make him a Jew, a Christian or a Zoroastrian.
- Muslim recorded from ʿIyāḍ ibn Ḥimār that the Prophet ﷺ reported Allah as saying that He created His servants ḥunafāʾ, pure in faith, but the devils came and led them away from their religion.

Taken together, the meaning is that Allah created His creatures so that some would later become believers and some disbelievers. In the beginning He made all His servants able to recognise Him and worship Him alone. They could know that none but He deserves worship. He took their covenant to act on that knowledge, which He placed in their minds and souls. He also decreed that some would be wretched and some happy. A hadith says that every person sets out at dawn to sell himself. Some free themselves by the bargain, and others ruin themselves.

Allah's decree will surely be carried out in His creation. He is the One "Who ordained precisely and inspired accordingly" (87:3). He is "the One Who has given everything its ˹distinctive˺ form, then guided ˹it˺" (20:50). The Two Ṣaḥīḥs report that those destined for happiness will find the deeds of the happy made easy for them. Those destined for misery will find the deeds of the miserable made easy for them. That is why Allah says here that He guided some while others were destined to stray, because they took the devils as patrons instead of Him.

### Does sincere error excuse a person?

This verse shows that ignorance of the Sharīʿah's injunctions is no valid excuse. If someone takes a wrong path in full sincerity, thinking it right, he is still not excused in Allah's sight. Allah has given everyone reason and common sense to tell true from false. Nor did He leave people to reason alone. He sent prophets and books that made right and wrong, truth and falsehood, perfectly clear.

Ibn Jarīr said this is one of the clearest proofs against those who claim Allah punishes no one for sins committed or errors believed until knowledge of the truth reaches him and he stubbornly turns from it. If that were so, he argued, there would be no difference between the misguided, who believe themselves guided, and those who really are guided. Yet Allah has distinguished the two in this verse, in both name and judgement.

Someone may object that a person acting in good faith, though mistaken, should bear no blame, because he does not know he is wrong. The answer is that Allah has blessed people with reason and sense, and with the teachings of the noble prophets as well. Through these, a person can at least measure his own way against the way they taught. There is bound to be some doubt, some twinge or question in his mind. His fault is that he ignored their teaching and kept to the wrong road he had taken.

Still, a person who searched for the truth as hard as he could, and never reached the right path or the true teaching, may be excused by Allah. Imam al-Ghazālī said so in his book Al-Tafriqah Bayn al-Islām wa al-Zandaqah.

### Following revered ancestors against the truth

People often lean on the great figures of the past in order to reject the one who calls them to the truth. The greatness of those forebears is established by history, and everyone takes it for granted that they were right. The one calling to the truth is new, with no history yet to vouch for him. A person looks at the ancients, revered as saints for their illustrious past, and compares them with this newcomer who has no tradition behind him. He then rejects the caller outright, sure that he himself is on the right path. This kind of misunderstanding is no excuse before Allah. In rejecting the caller he is not following Allah at all. He is only following Shayṭān in Allah's name.

### In short

- Allah's guidance was open to all. Some accepted it, and others earned error by taking the devils as patrons instead of Him.
- People are born on the fiṭrah, able to know Allah, yet His decree of happiness and misery is carried out, and each finds his chosen deeds made easy.
- Sincerely believing oneself guided is no excuse when reason and the prophets' teaching were available. Allah distinguishes the guided from the misguided in name and judgement.
- One who truly strove for the truth and still missed it may be excused, but clinging to revered ancestors against a caller to truth is following Shayṭān in Allah's name.

31.text:
This verse answers two customs of the pagan Arabs at once: "O Children of Adam! Dress properly whenever you are at worship. Eat and drink, but do not waste. Surely He does not like the wasteful". They counted circling the Kaʿbah naked as true worship and as reverence for Allah's House. They also used to go without food and drink during the days of Hajj. Ibn Jarīr reported that they ate only enough to stay alive and kept away in particular from ghee, milk and other pure foods. The verse was revealed against both practices.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O Children of Adam! Dress properly"** is literally "take your adornment" (zīnah). Ibn ʿAbbās explained that people used to circle the House naked, so Allah ordered them to take adornment. That means clean, proper clothes that cover the private parts. People were also commanded to wear their best clothes for every prayer. Other glosses are "put on what covers your nakedness" and "dress in clean, pure and beautiful clothes".

**"whenever you are at worship"** is literally "at every masjid". It means at every prayer, and when circling the Kaʿbah. Most explanations take masjid here in the sense of prostration (sajdah, sujūd).

**"Eat and drink"**: eat meat and fat, and drink milk, choosing whatever you like from the good things Allah has allowed. Eat and drink as you wish during the days of Hajj.

**"but do not waste."** Do not be excessive, and do not declare wholesome foods such as meat and fat unlawful. Do not go beyond what is permitted. ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī reported Ibn ʿAbbās as saying this concerns food and drink. Al-Bukhārī reported Ibn ʿAbbās as saying, in effect: eat what you like and wear what you like, so long as you avoid two things, extravagance and arrogance. Ibn Jarīr recorded through a ṣaḥīḥ chain that Ibn ʿAbbās said Allah has permitted eating and drinking, provided there is no waste or pride in it.

**"Surely He does not like the wasteful"**: those who abandon the lawful and run after the unlawful, and those who overstep the limits. Ibn Jarīr explained that Allah does not like people who cross the limits in what is allowed or in what is forbidden. They go to extremes in what He allowed, permit what He forbade, or forbid what He permitted. He likes the allowed to be treated as allowed, without excess, and the forbidden as forbidden. That is the justice He has commanded.

### Who was the verse revealed about?

Muslim, an-Nasāʾī and Ibn Jarīr recorded, in Ibn Jarīr's wording, that Ibn ʿAbbās described the idolaters going round the House naked, men by day and women by night. Women would say the words quoted under 7:28, and Allah replied with this verse. Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mujāhid, Qatādah, ʿAṭāʾ, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and as-Suddī said the same, as did Mālik from az-Zuhrī and several of the Salaf. All of them said the verse came down about the idolaters who circled the House naked.

The verse also struck at the second custom. Naked ṭawāf was immodest and ill-mannered. Its opposite, going without the good food Allah gave, with no valid excuse, had nothing to do with religion. Forbidding oneself what Allah has made lawful is effrontery and excess in worship, and Allah dislikes it. So eat and drink as you wish during Hajj, but without excess. Abstaining completely from lawful food is itself a kind of excess. So is forgetting the real purposes of Hajj and the remembrance (dhikr) of Allah, and doing nothing but eat and drink.

### Is the verse limited to its occasion?

The verse was revealed to end one custom of the Jāhiliyyah. Yet the scholars of tafsīr and the jurists of the Muslim Ummah agree unanimously that a command revealed about one event is not confined to that event. What counts is the generality of the words, and the command applies to everything those words cover. That is why most of the Companions and their Successors, and the mujtahid imams, drew many rulings from this verse.

### Can one pray without proper covering?

The most important ruling concerns ṣalāh. Naked ṭawāf is forbidden here, and the same ruling applies to prayer, which becomes ḥarām and void without covering. The Prophet ﷺ said that circling the House is a form of ṣalāh. Besides, since most explanations take masjid in this verse to mean sajdah, the verse plainly forbids nakedness in prostration. If it is forbidden in prostration, it is forbidden in every other position of the prayer: rukūʿ (bowing), qiyām (standing) and quʿūd (sitting). The Prophet's ﷺ statement makes this clearer still. A hadith in at-Tirmidhī adds that an adult woman's prayer is not valid without a proper covering for head and body, such as a khimār, ridāʾ, chādar, dupatta or large scarf.

Covering the body is obligatory outside prayer too. Other verses and hadiths prove it, among them the verse a little earlier: "clothing to cover your nakedness" (7:26). In sum, proper covering is the first human and Islamic duty on everyone, binding in every condition. In ṣalāh and ṭawāf it is obligatory in the highest degree.

### Should one dress well for prayer?

By calling clothing zīnah, adornment, the verse hints at more than bare covering. The preferred practice in prayer is to wear what adorns and looks fitting, within one's means. Ḥasan used to put on his best clothes for prayer. He would say, "Allah loves beauty, so I make myself beautiful for my Lord, for He has said, take your adornment at every masjid." So the verse proves two things. Covering is obligatory in prayer, and it is recommended and praiseworthy to wear neat, clean, good clothes there, within one's means.

This verse and the Sunnah encourage wearing one's best clothes for prayer, above all on Fridays and for the two ʿĪds. Men are also encouraged to put on perfume for prayer, as a part of adornment, and to use the siwāk, the tooth-stick, which rounds it off. The best colour for clothes is white. Imam Aḥmad recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told people to wear white, as among their best clothes, and to shroud their dead in it. He added that ithmid (antimony) is among the best kinds of kohl, since it clears the sight and helps the lashes grow. The chain is sound and its narrators meet Imam Muslim's conditions. Abū Dāwūd, at-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah also recorded it, and at-Tirmidhī called it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.

### How much must be covered?

Satr is the part of the body whose covering is farḍ at all times, and above all in prayer and ṭawāf. The Qur'an gave the command in brief and left the details to the Prophet ﷺ, who explained them. A man's satr runs from the navel to the knees. A woman's satr is her whole body except the face, the palms and the feet.

These details are all in the hadith narrations. If a man's body below the navel, or his knees, are bare, that way of dressing is a sin in itself, and his prayer is not properly performed in it. If a woman's head, neck, arms, shins or calves are bare, that way of dressing is not allowed in itself, and her prayer is not properly performed either. A hadith says that angels of good do not come to a home where a woman's head is uncovered.

The exemption of a woman's face, palms and feet means that their being uncovered causes no defect in her prayer. It does not mean she may go about with her face uncovered before non-maḥram men, those she may lawfully marry, without an excuse the Sharīʿah accepts.

Covering is a precondition of prayer, without which the prayer counts as not performed at all. And prayer asks for more than bare covering, since the verse speaks of zīnah. So it is makrūh, disliked, for a man to pray bareheaded or with his shoulders or elbows bare. That holds whether the shirt has half sleeves or is rolled up. Praying in clothes one would not wear in front of friends or in public is also makrūh. Examples are an undershirt alone, even with full sleeves, or a small cloth or handkerchief knotted round the head in place of a cap. No ordinary person would like to appear bareheaded before friends. How, then, could that be a fitting way to appear before Allah, the Master of all the worlds? This dislike is drawn from the word zīnah in the verse and from the Prophet's ﷺ explanations.

### What rulings come from "eat and drink, but do not waste"?

This sentence too was revealed against a single custom, the pagan belief that eating good food on Hajj was a sin. Its general words, though, yield many rulings.

Eating and drinking as needed is itself an obligation in the Sharīʿah. Someone who gives them up while able, until he dies or grows too weak to carry out his duties, is sinning and committing a crime in Allah's sight.

Al-Jaṣṣāṣ, in his Aḥkām al-Qurʾān, drew another ruling from the verse. In principle every food is permissible and ḥalāl unless a proof from the Sharīʿah shows that a particular thing is forbidden. The verse hints at this by not naming what is to be eaten and drunk. The masters of Arabic style have shown that leaving out the object in such a sentence signals generality. So one may eat and drink everything, except what has been declared ḥarām.

The last words, "do not waste", show that eating and drinking are not merely allowed but commanded, while excess in them is forbidden. Isrāf means crossing a limit, and it takes several forms.

- Crossing from the ḥalāl into the ḥarām, by eating and drinking forbidden things. That this is ḥarām is obvious.
- Treating what Allah made ḥalāl as ḥarām, without a reason the Sharīʿah accepts. Using the ḥarām is a sin, and in the same way, making the ḥalāl ḥarām is a revolt against Allah's law and a very grave sin.
- Eating and drinking beyond hunger and need. For this reason Muslim jurists (fuqahāʾ) have written that eating more than is needed to remove hunger is not permissible.
- Eating far less than needed, when one could eat, so that one grows weak and cannot carry out one's duties.

The Qur'an forbids both kinds of excess: "Surely the wasteful are ˹like˺ brothers to the devils" (17:27). Sūrat al-Furqān praises "those who spend neither wastefully nor stingily, but moderately in between" (25:67).

In all, eight rulings come out of this one sentence.

1. Eating and drinking as needed is obligatory.
2. Everything is ḥalāl unless a proof the Sharīʿah accepts shows it is forbidden.
3. Using what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden is isrāf and not allowed.
4. Treating as ḥarām what Allah made ḥalāl is isrāf and a grave sin.
5. Eating more once one is full is not allowed.
6. Eating so little that one becomes too weak for one's duties is isrāf.
7. Thinking about food and drink all the time is isrāf.
8. One need not have whatever one fancies the moment one fancies it.

### Why does moderation matter so much?

Imam Aḥmad recorded that al-Miqdām ibn Maʿdīkarib al-Kindī heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say that a human being fills no vessel worse than his own stomach. A few mouthfuls that keep his back upright are enough for him. If he must have more, let a third be for food, a third for drink, and a third left for breathing. An-Nasāʾī and at-Tirmidhī also collected this hadith. At-Tirmidhī called it ḥasan, or ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ according to another manuscript.

Al-Fārūq al-Aʿẓam told people to avoid eating and drinking too much, because it ruins the body, breeds disease and makes one sluggish. He urged moderation instead, as good for the body's health and far from waste. He also said that Allah does not like a fat scholar, meaning one who has grown heavy by overeating out of choice. And he said that a person is not ruined until he puts his own desires before his faith.

The righteous elders of the early period said that being busy with eating and drinking all the time also counts as isrāf. So does putting food before weightier matters, as if life had no worthier aim. Their saying is well known: eat to live, do not live to eat.

The Prophet ﷺ counted it as isrāf to satisfy every craving as soon as it arises. Ibn Mājah reported from Anas that he said it is waste to eat everything you desire. Al-Baihaqī reported that the Prophet ﷺ once saw ʿĀʾishah eating twice in one day. He asked her whether she would like eating to become her only pastime.

The call to moderation is not limited to food and drink. Moderation is very desirable in what one wears, where one lives and almost everything else. Ibn ʿAbbās's saying, given above, joins them: eat and drink as you like and wear what you like, avoiding only excess beyond need, and pride.

These rules carry religious benefit. Seen medically, a better prescription for health would be hard to find. Moderation in eating and drinking is a shelter from every disease.

### Half a verse of medicine

The caliph Hārūn ar-Rashīd had a Christian physician. He once said to ʿAlī ibn Ḥusayn ibn al-Wāqidī that the Qur'an contained nothing about medicine. Yet, he said, there are only two kinds of knowledge in our time: knowledge of religion, and knowledge of bodies, which is medicine. ʿAlī replied that Allah had put the whole of medicine into half a verse: "Eat and drink, but do not waste." The same saying is reported from some other early elders.

The physician then asked whether their Prophet had said anything about medicine. ʿAlī answered that the Prophet ﷺ had summed up medicine in a few sayings: that the stomach is the house of disease, that keeping away from what harms is the root of all medicine, and that each body should be given what it is used to. The physician said, "Your Book and your Prophet have left no medicine for Galen (Jālīnūs)."

Al-Baihaqī reported in Shuʿab al-Īmān, from Abū Hurairah, that the Prophet ﷺ called the stomach the body's reservoir. Every vein and nerve of the body draws from it. If the stomach is sound, the veins carry healthy nourishment back from it. If it is not, they spread disease through the body. Hadith experts (muḥaddithūn) have doubts about some of the wording in these narrations. All of them agree, though, on the stress on moderate eating and care found in countless hadiths.

### The inner reading: two kinds of adornment

In the language of learning, the adornment here is covering the private parts in prayer. In the language of unveiling, every servant's adornment lies in the station of contemplation. It is the heart being present, clinging to the Presence and witnessing the Ḥaqīqah without break. It has been said that the adornment of the worshipper's soul is the mark left by prostration, and the adornment of the knower's heart is the lights of finding. The worshipper wears servanthood in his prostration. The knower rests on the carpet of nearness in the calm of witnessing.

### In short

- The verse ended naked ṭawāf and the pagan habit of fasting from good food on Hajj, and its general words bind well beyond that occasion.
- Covering the body is always obligatory and is a precondition of prayer and ṭawāf. A man covers navel to knee, a woman all but her face, palms and feet.
- Good, clean clothes for prayer, within one's means, are recommended. Praying in clothes one would not wear in public is disliked.
- Everything is lawful until proven otherwise. Isrāf includes eating the forbidden, forbidding the lawful, overeating and starving oneself.
- Moderation in food is both part of religion and the root of good health.

32.text:
The rebuke continues against those who forbade what Allah allowed: "Ask, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Who has forbidden the adornments and lawful provisions Allah has brought forth for His servants?” Say, “They are for the enjoyment of the believers in this worldly life, but they will be exclusively theirs on the Day of Judgment. This is how We make Our revelations clear for people of knowledge.”" Some people forbid certain food, drink or clothing on their own judgement, without relying on what Allah has laid down. They add self-made restrictions to worship and call it obedience. So did the disbelievers of Makkah, who would not allow clothes in ṭawāf on Hajj and counted going without good, lawful food as worship.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Ask, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Who has forbidden"**: say this, O Muhammad, to the idolaters of Makkah who forbid things out of false opinion and invention. The question disowns them. It is a stern rebuke.

**"the adornments"**: the adornment Allah created, which includes garments. It covers wearing clothes during the days of pilgrimage, in the Sacred Precinct and while circling the Kaʿbah. In the pre-Islamic days they entered the Sacred Precinct completely naked, the men by day and the women by night.

**"and lawful provisions"**: aṭ-Ṭayyibāt, the good things of Allah's provision, delicious foods and drinks. They include meat and fat, which they used to forbid themselves during the days of pilgrimage. Allah made those practices unlawful.

**"Allah has brought forth for His servants?”"** Allah made them for the people who believe in Him and serve Him in this life. The disbelievers may share them for now, but that does not change whom they were made for.

**"Say, “They are for the enjoyment of the believers in this worldly life"**: for those who believe in Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an, though believer and sinner alike enjoy them in this world.

**"but they will be exclusively theirs on the Day of Judgment."** The word may be read khāliṣatun, "exclusively theirs", or khāliṣatan, describing their state. In the Hereafter the believers will have all of it to themselves, and no disbeliever will share in it, for Paradise is forbidden to the disbelievers. The good things are the believers' by right, even if others share them now.

**"This is how We make Our revelations clear for people of knowledge.”"** In this way Allah explains the Qur'an, setting out the lawful and the unlawful. He does it for people who reflect and believe it is from Him, since they are the ones who benefit. The verse refutes those whose excess and ignorance led them to think Allah is pleased when good clothes and good food are given up.

### Who decides what is lawful?

Declaring anything ḥalāl or ḥarām is the right of the Most Holy Being who created it, and no one else may interfere. Those who treat as ḥarām the good clothes and food Allah has allowed deserve His anger and punishment. Living in rags while having the means is no teaching of Islam. Nor, as some ignorant people think, is it something Islam holds up as a model.

### Did the early Muslims wear fine clothes?

Many of the early righteous elders and the imams of law, when Allah had given them means, often wore elegant and even costly clothes. The Prophet ﷺ himself, when his means allowed, wore the best of clothes. One narration says that he once came out wearing a cloak (ridāʾ) worth a thousand dirhams. Imam Abū Ḥanīfah is reported to have used a cloak worth four hundred guineas. Imam Mālik always wore decent and elegant clothes. Someone had taken it on himself to supply him with three hundred and sixty sets of clothes a year. Each set he wore for a single day and then gave to some poor student.

The reason is a saying of the Prophet ﷺ. When Allah gives a servant ample means, He likes to see the mark of His blessing on him, his clothing included. Letting that blessing show is a form of gratitude. Wearing worn-out or untidy clothes while having the means is ingratitude.

Two things must be guarded against, though: hypocrisy and showing off, and pride and arrogance. One should not dress well to impress others or to set oneself above them. The early elders were plainly free of such motives.

### Why did some of the best people dress simply?

The Prophet ﷺ, al-Fārūq al-Aʿẓam and some other Companions are reported to have worn plain or patched clothes. There were two reasons for this. First, they spent whatever income came to them on the poor and needy and on their religious aims, which left too little for fine clothes for themselves. Second, they were leaders of the people. They kept a simple and inexpensive appearance so that the well-off would take the hint, and so that ordinary people and the poor would not feel crushed by their standing.

The same holds for the noble Sufis, the rightly guided mystics who stress purifying the soul. When they make new seekers give up fine clothes and tasty food, they do not mean that giving these up for good earns merit (thawāb). It is a remedy, prescribed to rein in the self's unruly desires at the start of the search for truth. Once the seeker has learnt to master his desires and can no longer be lured into what is ḥarām, all the masters of the spiritual orders use and recommend good clothes and good food, like the early elders in general. At that stage these blessings become a means of knowing the Creator and drawing near Him. At the start they could have become obstacles, through ingratitude or the triumph of desire.

### What is the Sunnah in food and dress?

The basic way of the Prophet ﷺ, the Companions and the Tābiʿūn was not to fuss unnaturally over food and clothing. Whatever is easily to hand is good enough and should be used with gratitude. If the clothing is coarse and the food is dry, there is no need to strain after something better. One should not borrow for it, or brood over what is missing until it lands one in some other trouble.

In the same way, when good food and clothing come naturally, one should not go out of one's way to spoil them or avoid them. Chasing after fine food and clothes is a burden one lays on oneself. Its opposite, spoiling what is good and setting it aside for what is poor, is a self-imposed burden too, and a blameworthy one.

### Why do the good things belong to the believers?

The verse goes on to give the reason. All blessings, fine clothes and good food among them, were really created for obedient believers. Others enjoy them because of the believers, since this world is the place of deeds, not of rewards. Here no line is drawn between the genuine and the counterfeit, the good and the bad, where blessings are concerned. The feast is open to everyone, for the blessings come from al-Raḥmān, the All-Merciful to the whole world.

Yet the order of this world follows Allah's will, and His usual way here is this. When His obedient servants fall short in their duties to Him, others overpower them and seize the treasures of the world. The believers are then left in hunger and poverty. That law works only in this passing world of deeds. In the Hereafter every blessing and comfort will be kept for Allah's obedient servants. So the sentence means: tell them that all the blessings of this life are by right the believers' own, and on the Day of Qiyāmah they will be theirs alone.

Ibn ʿAbbās explained the verse differently. All the world's blessings and comforts belong by right to obedient believers alone, on condition that they do not become a source of trouble in the Hereafter. Disbelievers and sinners also receive these blessings in this life, often in greater measure. But for them the blessings will turn into ruin in the Hereafter, bringing punishment that lasts forever. Judged by the outcome, that is no comfort or honour anyone would want.

Others explain it in yet another way. Every blessing and comfort of this world comes mixed with endless striving, fear of decline and anxiety that never ends. Pure blessing and pure comfort do not exist here. Whoever receives blessings on the Day of Judgement will have them in perfect purity. There will be no toil for them, no fear of losing them and no worry after them. All three explanations fit the sentence, and that is why the Companions and the Tābiʿūn held to them.

### How should a believer use these gifts?

In the Hereafter Allah's bounties will come as a reward, and only those He sends to Paradise will receive them. The bounties of this world are different. They are available for a limited time, for the purpose of testing people. Each person receives his share as part of his own "test paper". The way to pass this test is not to keep away from the provisions Allah has given for it. It is to use them within the limits set for them. A person should answer Allah's blessings with gratitude, not with renunciation or a show of bravado.

### The inner reading: the adornments of Allah
